title: COGNITION IN ARCHITECTURAL AESTHETICS
central_proposition: Architectural design and aesthetics should be fundamentally rooted in human cognitive psychology, focusing on individual personality and needs to create spaces that align with human perception, emotion, and well-being.

concept_definitions.name: Cognition in Architectural Aesthetics
concept_definitions.definition: A Master thesis based on scientific research and self experience of architecture, society and urban planning, focusing on aesthetics and design in architecture to find solutions for problems in project development of future spaces where the main focus is on personality.

concept_definitions.name: Aesthetics
concept_definitions.definition: The only sphere with highly developed productive psychology on the fields of art and thus applicable to architecture.

concept_definitions.name: Perception
concept_definitions.definition: A tool for a man, his tool which does the architecture, allowing man to carve space as his mind tells him.

concept_definitions.name: Abstraction
concept_definitions.definition: Completion of past knowledge in a new form; actively drawing something away from somewhere and passively being drawn away from something.

concept_definitions.name: Generalization
concept_definitions.definition: Process of entity fragmentation into grouping in order to avoid complexity.

concept_definitions.name: Induction
concept_definitions.definition: Reasoning in which premises supply strong evidence for a probable conclusion.

concept_definitions.name: Deduction
concept_definitions.definition: Process of reasoning from one or more statements to reach a logically certain conclusion.

concept_definitions.name: Cognitive Map
concept_definitions.definition: Mental representations that store a person’s spatial knowledge of an environment.

concept_definitions.name: Quantity (in architecture)
concept_definitions.definition: Not understanding the number, but understanding sequences of abstract thinking without any number as well as values.

argument_structure: The paper begins by asserting the need for psychology in architecture, tracing historical shifts from human-centered design to machine-like production. It then delves into cognitive processes like perception, attention, abstraction, and memory, using examples from art and architecture to illustrate how these processes influence aesthetic judgment and design. It critiques current methodologies for neglecting cognitive aspects and proposes a framework where understanding human cognition is central to creating meaningful and effective built environments. The argument progresses from basic sensory input to complex intellectual operations, highlighting the interplay of conscious and unconscious processes.
mechanism_or_causal_logic: The core mechanism is that human cognitive processes (perception, attention, memory, abstraction, productive thinking) are fundamental drivers of aesthetic experience and architectural design. Environmental stimuli trigger these processes, leading to specific emotional responses, spatial understandings, and creative outputs. The paper posits that design decisions, whether conscious or unconscious, are shaped by these internal cognitive states and external influences. By understanding these mechanisms, architects can design spaces that better align with human needs, reduce cognitive load, enhance well-being, and foster creativity.

findings.antecedent: Quality of information (from different sensors like visual/sound)
findings.mechanism: Sound provides more possibilities for abstract and imaginary recreation than taste. Exact quality of information is required for recalling specific perceptions.
findings.quote: The quality of the given information is important for the effect of intelligent thinking. Rudolf Arnheim in his writings compare qualities of informations according different sensors based on taste and sound and it is sure that sound provides more possibilities to recall melodies that one has been affected to, but at the same time one can not recall the taste or compose it.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Implicitly refers to general psychological understanding, no specific study cited here.

findings.antecedent: Low variety of perceived elements (e.g., similar facades in large cities like Milan)
findings.mechanism: Insufficient unique visual elements (e.g., unique color, contrastive facades) make it hard for sensors to accrue enough information for accurate recall.
findings.quote: if you are passing through some of large cities as it is Milan, where variety of perceived elements are very low and often similar, you can not distinguish different spaces unless you spot the exact visual element of influence which can be a certain number of unique color or some contrastive designed façades.

findings.antecedent: Context from which information originates is different from typical context
findings.consequent: Difficulty distinguishing desired space / recalling right information
findings.mechanism: Sensors have difficulties recalling information when the environmental context is unfamiliar (e.g., different culture, language).
findings.quote: For example if one travels to a distant country with different culture, he will have difficulties to distinguish desired space mostly because the context he is observing is different from the context in which sensors are used to operate.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Observational example (traveling to a distant country).

findings.consequent: Adaptation/neglect of sensation; invention of additional similarities (psychosis/hallucinations in extreme cases)
findings.mechanism: Sensors adapt to constant repetition, leading to neglect or, in extreme cases, the brain inventing novel stimuli to break the monotony.
findings.quote: if a person is exposed to a constant repetition of sensations, consequently sensors will adapt to those repetitions as neglecting the sensation.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Hospitals using monophonic repetitions for psychoses, psychological methods of story repetition.

findings.antecedent: Insufficient stimuli for receptors (e.g., monotonous street facades)
findings.consequent: Difficulty recovering memories of past events/sights
findings.mechanism: Lack of unique or distinguishing information prevents the brain from forming strong memories or recalling them effectively.
findings.quote: This quality of informations may also lead to dangerous effects or insufficient stimuli for receptors, thus these facts should not appear in publicity, and especially in design of urban spaces.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Observational example (monotonous street facades in capitals).

findings.antecedent: Generic repetition of architectural context (e.g., static bridge, constant sun/hills)
findings.consequent: Wry visual image; psychological distress (as in 'The Scream')
findings.mechanism: Constant exposure to unchanging, repetitive environments can lead to sensory adaptation and psychological effects, potentially distorting perception.
findings.quote: the generic repetition of the architectural context as the fence on the side, the constant exposure to the static sun and hills view, lake which doesn’t change the shape even if body interact with the context, visual senses are giving the wry image.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Eduard Munch's 'The Scream' painting and his description.

findings.antecedent: Repetition in architectural design (e.g., Escher prints, pyramids, Mayan temples)
findings.mechanism: Repetitive patterns, when skillfully composed, can create visual illusions or a sense of innovation, especially when attention is drawn to transitions or subtractions of full/void.
findings.quote: If we take a glance to some of Escher prints we can easy spot how the repetition produces innovation (figure 02).
findings.empirical_support_cited: Escher prints, pyramids, Mayan temples, Gaudi's Casa Batllo, Gehry's designs.

mechanism_chain.description: A theoretical mechanism linking architectural features to cognitive outcomes and aesthetic experiences.

steps.from_construct: Architectural features (e.g., spatial configuration, material, light, soundscape)

steps.to_construct: Cognitive processing (e.g., attention allocation, pattern recognition, memory encoding)
Aesthetic experience / Recall of perceptions (e.g., possibilities to recall melodies/perceptions)

theory_commitments.specific_claim: Architectural aesthetics are mediated by specific cognitive processes such as perception, attention, memory, and information processing.

theory_commitments.theory_name: Environmental Psychology Theories (e.g., Information Processing Theory)
theory_commitments.specific_claim: The quality and complexity of sensory information from architectural environments influence cognitive load and subsequent aesthetic judgments.
